entries.title: Patient interview — competitive tennis player
entries.topic: cartilage injury in a competitive tennis player
tags: cartilage injury in a competitive tennis player
entries.summary: the participant described long-term discomfort after his injuries, the lack of early intervention and the burden of two hours of daily rehabilitation. The interview confirmed the need for focal cartilage repair and led us to develop a smart rehabilitation mirror that corrects exercise posture at home.
entries.rationale: After our survey showed that focal cartilage defects are a common form of hyaline cartilage injury, we looked for a high-risk group to interview and approached a key member of the Zhejiang University tennis team with ten years of competitive play.
entries.interview: He described two major sprains. After the first, a CT showed obvious cartilage damage, but with no good early treatment he was sent home with painkillers; rehabilitation through a rehabilitation physician and TCM physiotherapy took about two hours a day — “and that was with a team doctor” — yet helped only partially. A teammate who ruptured an ACL received an artificial ligament and recovered quickly, but the hard implant kept wearing the remaining cartilage, and doctors had no solution.
entries.integration: The interview confirmed focal defects as a key target and pushed us to design a material that fits all kinds of hyaline cartilage injury. The pain point of slow, cumbersome rehabilitation led us to the idea of improving the rehabilitation experience, which later became the AI-guided smart mirror developed with Lin Lei's group in biomedical engineering.

entries.title: Patient interviews — post-operative experiences
entries.summary: The three post-operative patients described persistent pain, limited function and the extra burden of having their invisible pain dismissed. The interviews moved us to address the psychological and social side of treatment through science videos, public lectures and rehabilitation discussions with medical students.
entries.rationale: We met one participant at the iGEM East China meet-up and found one participant and another participant through a Xiaohongshu discussion thread; all three had direct experience of post-operative cartilage injury.
entries.interview: one participant had ACL reconstruction; her doctors said the artificial ligament recovers faster but is harder and keeps wearing the cartilage, with no good answer for the resulting damage. one participant developed osteoarthritis after patellar surgery; follow-up visits concluded that her discomfort was normal, and her rehabilitation doctor said the persistent friction caused by the protruding bone position is mechanical and irreversible, and that further surgery could cause other problems. another participant's wrist surgery affected her function even more. They described anxiety, irritability and self-blame because the joint is internal and leaves no visible scar for others to see.
entries.integration: We recognised that doctors' neglect and patients' psychological burden deserve attention, and that the environment around patients has to change. We ran public lectures on cartilage health, reflected on the structural causes of neglect from an anthropological perspective, wrote two survey reports and held a roundtable with medical students on rehabilitation.

entries.title: Patient interview — rural access to care
entries.topic: cartilage care in a remote village
tags: cartilage care in a remote village
entries.summary: The Yantan village visit revealed long travel distances to care, chronic joint problems managed with painkillers and low awareness of cartilage health. We wrote these observations on rural access into our survey report and pushed for community cartilage screening and education.
entries.rationale: To understand regional differences in care, we visited Yantan village — a small, seasonal-tourism village with many left-behind elderly people and limited transport. We spent most time with an elderly man who lives by manual labour.
entries.interview: He has had arthritis for more than five years and still suffers from it; he manages it with local herbal medicine and painkillers. He described repeated trips to hospitals and said the nearest one is an hour's drive; township hospitals can handle acute problems but have little for chronic disease — “let alone a small illness like mine.”
entries.integration: We wrote these observations into our survey report and turned it into a professional report for the Hangzhou Municipal Health Commission, which will guide grassroots organisations in screening for and publicising cartilage health in the region.

entries.title: Dr. Huang Jun
entries.topic: sports-medicine advice from a national team doctor
tags: sports-medicine advice from a national team doctor
entries.summary: Dr. Huang Jun started from athletes' needs and pointed out the limits of an operating-room injection, portability and quick recovery. The interview pushed us to explore acute-repair materials and drug-carrying modules that speed conservative treatment and reduce overtreatment.
entries.rationale: We wanted authoritative advice on sports injuries caused by cartilage defects, so we consulted Dr. Huang Jun, head of the joint department at Zhejiang Provincial Sports Hospital, a member of the sports-medicine branch of the Zhejiang Medical Doctor Association, and a former team doctor for the national gymnastics team and at the Asian Games.
entries.interview: He believes the project has strong application potential, but for athletes it must be more portable and easier to operate; the surgical-injection route keeps the material in the operating room. He also said that programmability fits athletes' needs well, and described cases in which athletes over-treated in order to restore function quickly.
entries.integration: We adopted the advice and decided to develop later materials better suited to acute repair — usable for athletes and in extreme team or field settings — and to consider carrying immune factors or drugs in the functional modules to speed conservative treatment; this became a key consideration for the module payload.

entries.title: Dr. Qiu Xiaoming
entries.organisation: Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Hangzhou
entries.summary: Dr. Qiu Xiaoming pointed out that different joints bear different loads and need tunable strength. The interview led us to tune SELP through the 2KY repeat number and to match different defects with modelling.
entries.rationale: The first step of NEST was to choose a filler that meets the complex requirements of cartilage repair — filling the defect directly and relieving pain immediately. Dr. Qiu Xiaoming is an orthopaedic doctor at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital in Hangzhou with extensive clinical experience and academic work, so we visited him.
entries.interview: We presented the first SELP design — a single fixed set of 2KY5, 2KY10 and 2KY16 proteins. He said that the elbow, knee and other joints bear different loads and need different strengths, and that a single-strength material could not achieve our goal of treating all hyaline cartilage defects. We proposed tuning the 2KY repeat number through sequence design to change the material's strength and toughness; he agreed.
entries.integration: Our literature work showed that higher repeat numbers reduce pore size and raise cell adhesion, favouring GAG production, native cartilage growth and anti-inflammatory signalling, and fitting patients with different immune capacities and defect sizes. We decided to build a programmable repeat-number method and to model real cartilage to fix the hydrogel's final properties, achieving SELP as a broad treatment platform.

entries.title: Dr. Li Zhiguo
entries.topic: the diagnostic gap in early cartilage injury
entries.organisation: Beijing Tongren Hospital, Mentougou campus (as recorded in IHP)
tags: the diagnostic gap in early cartilage injury
entries.summary: Dr. Li Zhiguo described patients with clear discomfort who do not meet clinical intervention standards. The interview confirmed the need to fill defects early and prompted us to verify the biocompatibility of non-autologous materials.
entries.rationale: Dr. Li Zhiguo is an orthopaedic physician in the joint department of Beijing Tongren Hospital's Mentougou campus and an authority on osteoarthritis with extensive surgical experience. We wanted to understand the inversion behind the sparse records — many cartilage-injury cases but few documented — and to have our first design assessed for feasibility.
entries.interview: He spoke with us by phone. He acknowledged that many patients have obvious discomfort after a cartilage defect but do not reach the imaging findings or inflammatory markers needed for drug treatment, and a large share have strong discomfort below the clinical intervention threshold. The definition of cartilage injury itself is disputed within the field; he has seen patients move between hospitals receiving diagnoses that ranged from rehabilitation and no treatment to surgery, and that blurred boundary is why epidemiological studies are scarce. He sees strong potential in our material: many joint diseases progress chronically, and treatments after the threshold — joint replacement, for example — bring many rehabilitation problems, so interrupting the process early would greatly help patients. Some patients reject conservative options such as microfracture because they rely on the body's own recovery and take a long time, and some ask for more aggressive treatment simply to recover faster. Our material is relatively non-invasive, simple to operate and relieves discomfort immediately, which can improve adherence to conservative treatment. In shoulder dislocation, patellar fracture and ACL reconstruction he has seen patients' self-adaptation aid recovery, and he particularly stressed the biocompatibility of non-autologous materials.
entries.integration: The conversation confirmed our observation and pushed us to investigate the causes of the inversion. Following his advice we ran biocompatibility tests, with good results.

entries.title: Dr. Ren Bo
entries.summary: Dr. Ren Bo warned that material complexity and age-related immune differences affect repair. The interview focused us on hyaline cartilage defects, led to a dose-adjustable immune module, and strengthened cartilage-health education for younger people.
entries.rationale: Dr. Ren Bo is director of the sports-medicine centre at Xi'an Honghui Hospital and a member of ICRS and APKASS, with expertise in immune research on biomimetic and regenerative cartilage. We sought his help on the linker connection and modular design.
entries.interview: He was concerned about the material's complexity: many fillers for early cartilage defects are challenged at the production and mammalian-testing stages. He stressed that immune capacity differs between older and younger patients — older patients' wear often begins with long-term poor exercise habits when they were young, but high hormone levels and strong immunity allowed repair without obvious symptoms until moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis developed, and immune recovery is a persistent difficulty when treating older patients. He said the product should be specified for hyaline cartilage injury rather than cartilage in general, because cartilage also includes bone-cartilage and other immunologically active parts. He acknowledged the blurriness of cartilage treatment and the early-treatment gap, and stressed public education on cartilage health from a young age, including exercise habits and posture.
entries.integration: We later contacted Dr. Huang Wenwen for animal-experiment discussions on material complexity. We began designing an immune module and settled on liposome-encapsulated mitochondria or immune factors for personalised treatment; the linker system lets us control the immune-module dose, giving older and younger patients different doses with no extra production line — only different protein-powder blending ratios. Inspired by Dr. Ren we ran community cartilage-health outreach and turned the experience into a survey report that can influence government.

entries.title: Dr. Zhang Yumei
entries.topic: where the material fits alongside rehabilitation
entries.organisation: First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University
tags: where the material fits alongside rehabilitation
entries.summary: Dr. Zhang Yumei defined the patients for whom the material complements conservative rehabilitation and warned that unsupervised home training with poor form can worsen wear. The interview led to the rehabilitation-mirror concept, which uses movement correction to reduce ongoing damage.
entries.rationale: Almost everyone we interviewed had been through rehabilitation, so we asked a rehabilitation physician about clinical practice. Dr. Zhang Yumei of Nanjing Medical University's First Affiliated Hospital has extensive experience in post-operative cartilage injury and early-to-mid osteoarthritis rehabilitation.
entries.interview: Conservative exercise rehabilitation is indeed first-line for small, shallow cartilage contusions and for cartilage damage after ligament reconstruction with bone-tunnel wear — cases that do not meet surgical indications. Not all cartilage injuries repair themselves: young patients with small contusions can partly recover after abnormal load is removed and alignment corrected, but severe or large-area wear has very limited self-repair even in the young, and older patients' degenerated matrix hardly repairs spontaneously. Doctors differ widely because classification, area, depth, ligament or meniscus involvement and activity demands vary; the same images can lead a sports-medicine doctor and a general orthopaedic doctor to different strategies. Rehabilitation usually takes three to six months, occasionally up to a year. She does not recommend home rehabilitation for most patients: much wear comes from incorrect alignment, and unsupervised training with poor form can worsen the damage. She sees the material not as a replacement for surgery but for conservative-treatment patients — cartilage wear after ligament surgery (possibly broadening to knee post-operative cases), shallow small defects, and focal wear in early-to-mid osteoarthritis — used together with exercise rehabilitation.
entries.integration: Dr. Zhang inspired us to build a mirror that guides home rehabilitation and helps patients correct their movements. It fills the treatment gap during our product's long market timeline and helps avoid repeated wear from incorrect alignment after injection. She is very willing to serve as medical advisor for our rehabilitation project.

entries.title: Nurse Xue Han and her nursing team
entries.topic: redesigning the hardware around the ward
tags: redesigning the hardware around the ward
entries.summary: The nursing team — 18 people including Xue Han — gave feedback on workflow, training and device compatibility. Their input led to the integrated endoscope and instrument, the electronic manual and Bluetooth screen mirroring, and a syringe-damping blind test that improved precise dosing.
entries.rationale: The hardware is used by clinical staff, so we took our first design to a professional nursing team rather than deciding its details internally. Xue Han is an experienced nurse who spent ten years at 254 Hospital and rotated through several departments; our design drew mainly on the advice of her and her colleagues — 18 in total.
entries.interview: They raised three main issues: uncertainty about where and how the material is prepared; questions about the experience of using the device; and the training complexity of introducing a new device, plus adaptability concerns — if the interface is not common, the endoscopic view cannot be shown on emergency-room screens.
entries.integration: We combined the endoscope and the operating instrument, added an electronic manual, and moved the display connection to Bluetooth to fit existing hospital equipment and reduce cost. We also ran a blind test of syringes with different damping with the nursing team and chose the final syringe (see the syringe questionnaire ).

entries.title: Prof. Ouyang Hongwei
entries.topic: defining the indication and the degradation window
tags: defining the indication and the degradation window
entries.summary: Prof. Ouyang Hongwei helped us narrow the indication to focal, partial-thickness cartilage defects and early degeneration, and required degradation to match tissue regeneration. The interview led to degradation curves that clarify the platform's treatment boundary.
entries.rationale: NEST began as an injectable, in-situ hydrogel, but internally “cartilage repair” and “treating osteoarthritis” were used almost interchangeably. We consulted Prof. Ouyang Hongwei to clarify the repair scenario and the boundary of the indication.
entries.interview: He raised three points: repair is not just filling a defect, because the material enters a continuously degenerating microenvironment; degradation must keep pace with new tissue formation and bond reliably to the surrounding cartilage; and we must specify which scenario we target — focal partial-thickness defects, early degeneration, or advanced OA with subchondral bone changes. He was clear that local repair cannot be equated with reversing osteoarthritis at every stage.
entries.integration: We reversed the order of our claims: NEST targets focal, partial-thickness cartilage defects and post-traumatic or early degenerative stages, while advanced OA appears only as the downstream consequence in the background. Degradation became a designed parameter: we added degradation curves in PBS, collagenase/protease solution and simulated synovial fluid at 4, 8 and 12 weeks alongside ITC purification, compression and lap-shear testing. The curves showed that material degradation and cartilage regeneration are largely complementary, so no separate degradation module was needed. After the conversation, Prof. Ouyang built an advisory team for us and suggested we continue with Dr. Hong Yi and Dr. Yi Junzhi in his laboratory, who guided the following experiments and design.

entries.title: Songlin Shi
entries.topic: questioning the magnetic and protein routes
tags: questioning the magnetic and protein routes
entries.summary: Songlin Shi questioned the trade-off between magnetic particle orientation and clearance, and the reliability of protein performance after denaturation and refolding. The interview led to a low-field, fast-crosslinking scheme and to ITC purification that protects protein structure.
entries.rationale: We met Songlin Shi — a doctoral researcher at the Emergency Medicine Research Centre of Westlake University's School of Medicine, a community mentor, a former member of the CCiC steering committee, an HP Committee member and an iGEM BYLP — while the three functional modules were taking shape but their compatibility, hardware support and protein feasibility had not been thought through.
entries.interview: His questions focused on two areas: the tension between nanoparticle anisotropy and iron metabolism — enough magnetic loading for orientation versus particles that must eventually be cleared — and protein feasibility, including whether structure survives denaturation and renaturation and whether β-sheet aggregation and inclusion bodies would block the project.
entries.integration: We abandoned the idea of pulling particles with a large coil field and built the current scheme on anchoring and speed: Fe₃O₄-binding peptides anchor particles to the SELP network so a low external field can orient both together, Ru/SPS crosslinking fixes the orientation in about two seconds, and the procedure became injection—observation—magnetic orientation—blue-light crosslinking. For production we chose ITC purification, which relies on SELP's reversible phase behaviour and keeps the protein natively folded rather than denaturing and refolding it.

entries.title: Prof. Patrick Butaye
entries.summary: Prof. Butaye advised validating SELP expression and phase behaviour at small scale before scaling up. The team completed expression and ITC-purification validation accordingly, lowering the risk of discovering protein problems only after large batches.
entries.rationale: The whole NEST route rested on an unverified assumption — that SELP, a large, highly repetitive protein, could be expressed normally in E. coli. We asked Prof. Patrick Butaye — vice-dean of City University of Hong Kong's Jockey Club College of Veterinary Medicine and Life Sciences, adjunct professor at Ghent University, editor-in-chief of Veterinary Sciences and an invited expert for WHO and EFSA — whether expression would work and whether abnormal folding or membrane issues should be expected.
entries.interview: He advised a small-scale trial first and gave detailed experimental guidance; he considered the design essentially sound and sent useful reference papers by email. We also visited his laboratory, whose display boards of published work gave us ideas for our own poster.
entries.integration: We split expression into two steps: confirm at small volume whether the protein is expressed, in what form and with the expected phase behaviour, then scale up in E. coli BL21. ITC purification later confirmed soluble protein with normal phase behaviour, answering both the expression and the structural concerns; the route was further corrected by Weixinkang and Prof. Huang Wenwen.

entries.title: Prof. Huang Wenwen
entries.summary: Prof. Huang Wenwen pointed out that residual salt from ITC purification hinders photocrosslinking. We added dialysis to remove it, solved the gelation problem, reached about two-second visible-light gelation, and now optimise purification and gelation as one continuous flow.
entries.rationale: NEST makes SELP chain length, domain ratio, functional residues and peptide interfaces designable parameters. We asked Prof. Huang Wenwen, a tenured associate professor at the Zhejiang University–University of Edinburgh Institute (ZJE) and a leading researcher in the SELP field, about platform scalability and about the process link between purification and rapid photocrosslinking.
entries.interview: She rated the overall design highly: the platform lets the team combine or adjust functions on a shared scaffold to meet different patient needs. She focused on the relation between crosslinking efficiency and the purification conditions, noting that the salt added during ITC can remain and interfere with Ru/SPS crosslinking; she also compared our purification efficiency with her laboratory's process and encouraged further industrial exploration.
entries.integration: We kept the shared-scaffold, standard-interface, replaceable-module architecture and added a dialysis step after ITC to remove residual salt. After the change, SELP reached visible-light gelation in about two seconds, turning her advice into a verifiable process improvement and showing that purification and gelation must be optimised as one continuous flow.

entries.title: Dr. Yi Junzhi
entries.summary: Dr. Yi Junzhi required modularity to be proven by assembly efficiency, function retention and reproducibility. The interview led us to a high-efficiency ligation system, a comparison of tag insertion positions, and a flexible linker to reduce steric shielding.
entries.rationale: “Modules can be plugged in” was still a claim on a design drawing: the scaffold stays, the functional units change, but we could not say what proved it. We consulted Dr. Yi Junzhi, a researcher at Zhejiang University's Liangzhu Laboratory working on modular protein engineering and bone tissue engineering.
entries.interview: He agreed that sequence-level design and standardised interfaces help tune material properties, but asked whether modules affect one another: fusion peptides may change expression or solubility, tags and ligases may change conformation, and multiple modules may cause site masking, lower ligation efficiency or weaker function. Plug-and-play should be proven by assembly efficiency, function retention and reproducibility, not by a diagram.
entries.integration: We made assembly efficiency the first criterion and chose the SnoopTag/SnoopLigase route, building on the lighter SnoopLigase 2 toolkit (SnoopLigase2, SnoopTag2, DogTag2), which couples efficiently in standard PBS. We kept two insertion options — SnoopTag2 at the SELP terminus for first-round validation, or inside a domain for more flexible assembly — with an optional flexible linker to reduce steric hindrance. The 12- and 23-amino-acid tags keep the structural burden small and can also be inserted internally.

entries.title: Prof. Lin Si'en
entries.topic: from particle alignment to a real anisotropic network
entries.organisation: University of Hong Kong (as recorded in IHP)
tags: from particle alignment to a real anisotropic network
entries.summary: Prof. Lin Si'en distinguished particle orientation, network orientation and direction-dependent mechanics, showing each must be verified separately. The interview led us to a magnetic-particle-binding peptide that anchors particles to the SELP scaffold and transmits the field force.
entries.rationale: Our early magnetic module simply mixed Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles into the SELP precursor, applied a field and crosslinked — with no anchoring mechanism and no plan to prove that anything had aligned. We asked Prof. Lin Si'en at the University of Hong Kong how structural orientation becomes measurable tissue-engineering function.
entries.interview: He focused on evidence: particles aligning does not automatically prove a stable anisotropic SELP network, let alone reproduce native cartilage mechanics — particle orientation, network orientation and direction-dependent gel properties must each be shown. He listed five variables that affect orientation (field strength and gradient, particle concentration, ligation efficiency, precursor rheology, crosslinking timing) and separated “a directional structure formed” from “that structure changed cell behaviour.”
entries.integration: His point that particle orientation is not network orientation directly produced the Fe₃O₄-binding peptide. Modelling by Wu Jialin and Sun Yuxuan showed that unanchored particles cannot keep SELP molecules aligned, even with charge tuning through lysine, so we anchor the particles to the SELP scaffold and let a low field orient particles and network together. Two selected 7-mer peptides, HYIDFRW and TVNFKLY, were validated to bind Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles, and TVNFKLY can be fused in tandem with other functional peptides while keeping its binding ability. The magnetic module then joined the SnoopTag2/DogTag interface, and the operation became a fixed sequence — injection, confirmation, magnetic orientation, blue-light crosslinking — with an independently controlled light source in the endoscope module.

entries.title: Prof. Li Xiaoming
entries.topic: linking field-induced structure to local mechanics
tags: linking field-induced structure to local mechanics
entries.summary: The discussion with Prof. Li Xiaoming connected the magnetic field, structural orientation and local mechanical response, leading to a four-phase model that includes the crosslinking sequence. The model guides sampling; YAP/TAZ cell responses still require separate validation.
entries.rationale: We wanted to connect external-field control, structural change and the local mechanical environment that cells sense, so that modelling could guide experiments. Prof. Li Xiaoming is a professor at Beihang University's School of Biological Science and Medical Engineering and vice-chair of the Intelligent Biomimetic Materials branch of the Chinese Society for Biomaterials. His team's Advanced Science paper, “Biomimetic Gradient Hydrogels Regulate Osteochondral Regeneration Microenvironment Remodeling via Spatiotemporal Programming Engineering”, drew our attention, and we contacted him online.
entries.interview: Because his work uses electric fields while our system responds to magnetic fields through Fe₃O₄ and SELP, the model had to be rebuilt around our mechanism. The discussion divided “the field changes hydrogel properties” into steps that can be analysed: how the field affects orientation, how crosslinking preserves it, and how the fixed structure changes local mechanical response.
entries.integration: Our Model reflects this: alongside molecular dynamics and network analysis, we built a four-phase continuum model describing SELP–Fe₃O₄ fibres, non-fibrous matrix, free particles and water, and included the preparation sequence. The model now predicts local material environments that can guide sampling and later cell-response comparisons, including YAP/TAZ readouts.

entries.title: Prof. Wu Congjun
entries.summary: Prof. Wu Congjun helped distinguish the filling and orientation window before illumination from the fast fixation required after it. The workflow now fixes injection, observation and magnetic orientation before the blue light, with an independently controlled light source.
entries.rationale: NEST's precursor must stay flowable for injection and shaping, then form a stable network on demand. We discussed with Prof. Wu Congjun, Chair Professor of Physics at Westlake University, how blue light should trigger crosslinking and when it should be switched on.
entries.interview: We described the Ru/SPS visible-light system, which crosslinks tyrosine residues and gels in about two seconds under blue light. The discussion clarified two separate requirements: an operating window before illumination for filling and orientation, and rapid fixation after it. Illuminating too early loses flow; too late risks precursor loss or structural change.
entries.integration: We made injection and photocrosslinking separately controlled steps and fixed the order injection—confirmation—magnetic orientation—blue-light crosslinking, keeping the magnetic field on while the light is applied. The endoscope module has an independently controlled blue-light source so the operator can inspect the defect and fill first, and the software flow presents the illumination and gelation steps explicitly.

entries.title: Dr. Hong Yi
entries.summary: Dr. Hong Yi split the vague idea of adhesion into wet-state bonding, shape retention and long-term interface integration, prompting lap-shear, compression and rheology tests and a clearer covalent mechanism for bonding to host cartilage.
entries.rationale: We assumed that because SELP gels, fills the defect and looks attached, adhesion was solved. The joint environment is wet and cyclically loaded, so we asked Dr. Hong Yi, a researcher at Zhejiang University's Liangzhu Laboratory working on biomimetic cartilage and medical tissue adhesives, to examine the interface.
entries.interview: He asked what “adhesion” means here: the material's wet adhesive strength, the gel's shape retention, or long-term stable integration with native cartilage — related but different properties. A single tensile or compression test cannot represent cyclic loading, wear, interfacial peeling and post-degradation change, and adhesion, modulus and toughness trade off against each other.
entries.integration: “Adhesion” became three things with three tests: compression for mechanical support and shape retention, lap-shear for interfacial bonding to cartilage, and rheology for precursor flow and gelation — alongside ITC purification. The interface claim also became chemical: the engineered tyrosine residues can couple covalently with endogenous tyrosine, so bonding is not only physical or mechanical interlocking.

entries.title: Prof. Chen Ming
entries.summary: Across four meetings, Prof. Chen Ming required clear variables, model assumptions and experimental evidence. The team split five design variables, assigned each modelling scale its question, and calibrated predictions with rheology, gelation and directional mechanics.
entries.rationale: We expected modelling to tell us directly which sequence was best and saw the software mainly as a display. We asked Prof. Chen Ming at Zhejiang University whether that view holds up from a systems-modelling and data-analysis perspective.
entries.interview: He focused on whether variables are clearly defined, whether model inputs and outputs are interpretable, and whether results are supported by independent experiments. A prediction without stated assumptions, parameter ranges and error sources is hard to trust, and building a software interface is not model validation: software should help record parameters, compare options, show the basis of a model and feed results into the next design round.
entries.integration: We separated the simulations so that each of the five variables has a single dependent variable that can be tested on its own, assigned each scale a question (all-atom MD and enhanced sampling for conformations and functional-site states; coarse-grained Martini 3.0 networks for crosslinked mechanics; magnetic–mechanical coupling for field and particle effects), and paired every model with calibration or validation experiments — gelation time, rheology, compression, structural imaging and directional mechanical tests. The four rounds of discussion also led us to choose the Model track as one of our Best Award applications this year.

entries.title: Dr. Shen Yang
entries.topic: pain that falls outside the diagnostic threshold
tags: pain that falls outside the diagnostic threshold
entries.summary: Dr. Shen Yang helped us turn the interviews into a systematic anthropological study of why early joint symptoms remain medically invisible. The work became a paper discussed at an ethnographic workshop and fed back to Zhejiang University's health-services institute, and it shaped our medical-humanities lectures for future doctors.
entries.rationale: Our surveys and interviews showed how cartilage damage is overlooked in the medical system. We wanted to examine the structural reasons behind this invisibility and how it might be addressed at the system level, so we approached Dr. Shen Yang — a researcher in Zhejiang University's Department of Sociology and a Boston University PhD in anthropology — at the university's Third Annual Social Research Conference.
entries.interview: She advised us to study the topic systematically and produce a paper, and after a semester of coursework we wrote “Pain beyond the diagnostic threshold: the medical invisibility of early joint symptoms”. Starting from the inversion between many reported symptoms and few formal records, and drawing on Kleinman's distinction between disease and illness and on Carel and Kidd's framework of epistemic injustice, the paper examines how patients' accounts of pain, activity limitation and disruption to daily life are translated into clinically recognisable information, and which experiences are lost in that translation. It argues that care needs can still be identified and answered while a diagnosis remains uncertain, and that understanding this problem requires attention to diagnostic uncertainty, the patient's situation and the organisation of care. Its contribution is to move attention from the number of diagnoses to the burden of symptoms that are not yet fully recorded, and to propose including patient-reported pain, life impact and follow-up needs in assessment. It also considers structural violence and the power imbalance inherent in doctor–patient relationships.
entries.integration: We took the paper to the ethnographic workshop in Chiang Mai and fed the results back to Zhejiang University's Institute of Social Medicine and Health Services Management. We also ran medical-anthropology lectures and seminars that raised future doctors' patient awareness — that illness is not only a physiological injury but is accompanied by social context and structural violence — and called for patients' care needs to be recognised even within ambiguous diagnostic standards.

He also shared his experience of drawing with visual sensors and allowed us to present a new piece that traces the movement of engineered bacteria, which made our synthetic-biology talks more interactive and helped audiences understand engineered bacteria.
